stories.title: The Physics Illusion
stories.description: Ajay discusses the 'physics illusion' in social sciences—the belief that there are single grand theories universally applicable. He notes that modern economics has shifted away from this towards solving one puzzle at a time with specific datasets, acknowledging that context matters (e.g., understanding diabetes in India might be different from China).

stories.title: Mendel's 40 Copies
stories.description: Ajay shares a trivia fact that Gregor Mendel ordered 40 copies of his paper from the printer to disseminate it. This highlights the contrast with the modern world where electronic dissemination is instant but getting attention is the real challenge.

stories.title: The Rising Price of Husbands
stories.description: Amit mentions a paper by Vijayendra Rao with this title (about dowry) as an example of a brilliant, clever title that is also accurate to the content.

stories.title: Jeff Bezos vs. Slideshows
stories.description: Amit contrasts Ajay's 'slideshow as development platform' method with Jeff Bezos's famous ban on PowerPoint at Amazon. He clarifies that Ajay's method is for internal brainstorming and structuring, not for simplifying or dumbing down ideas for an audience.

recommendations.comment: Amit quotes from this book by Lawrence H. White in the intro, using a metaphor about the structure of intellectual production.
Amit mentions Malcolm Gladwell's book regarding the 'relative age effect' in sports, explaining why he (born in December) had no chance in sports.
Amit recommends Deirdre McCloskey's book 'Economical Writing: Thirty-Five Rules for Clear and Concise Prose' for learning how to write about complex subjects for a lay audience.
Ajay recommends 'Strunk and White' as universal knowledge for anyone who wants to write.
Ajay recommends Amit Varma's writing course.
Ajay mentions this as a peer-reviewed research journal he co-edits, which follows the IMRD structure.

core_ideas.description: A good paper must have: 1) A clear Question, 2) A persuasive Answer (substantiated by work), and 3) Novelty (it must be new).
The standard structure for STEM papers: Introduction (what is known, questions), Methods (what was done, replicable detail), Results (what was found), Discussion (implications).
Ajay's method of using a detailed slideshow (not for presentation) to brainstorm, refine, and structure the paper with a team before writing the prose. It serves as a 'skeleton' for the paper.
Writing the paper is not enough. You must disseminate it (blogs, op-eds, small conferences). 'It is far better to get 10 good people in a room... than a shallow engagement with large numbers.'
Writing is not just recording thoughts; it's a process of discovery. You might start sailing for India and discover America. You must be willing to throw away drafts and rewrite.
